I think that there are many things that trump is doing that he doesn't want to do, but was part of his promise to the people when he ran. Healthcare is one of those, and all the evangelical crap is another. He needed to do these things in order to be elected, and he is following through with his promises as best he can.

People are focusing too much on "who is going to pay for our healthcare that is 10x the price of what it should be", and not enough on "we should reduce the cost of healthcare". Allow any company to make generics, allow all medications that were developed with federal funds to be generic. Find if the FDA is creating barriers of entry into markets that have nothing to do with patient safety (hint, they are). Remove the power of the AMA, a private entity, and allow people to use their own judgement If a hospital only wants to hire AMA approved doctors and nurses, that is one thing; if someone wants a retired doctor who's "license" has lapsed to give them medical advice, that's another.
I'd go a step further and say anything developed with public funds should automatically be in the public domain, and I mean anything. Cap patents on drugs at 5 years.

Another would be reforming the entire medical insurance industry. It's really really bizarre how it works.

Who decides how much a doctor at his own practice gets paid for a given procedure? It's not the doctor. When they perform a given procedure (or just have a consultation or whatever) they bill the insurance company. The insurance company then pays them (sometimes months later) whatever they think that procedure is worth. Private insurance tends to pay doctors far more than medicare which in turn pays far more than medicaid.

Instead of concerning themselves with competitive pricing, this incentivizes doctors into ensuring they charge enough to hit the max fee that the insurance will reimburse. It also means that instead of all customers being equal, private customers will result in more revenue for the hospital or practice. This recently came to light with Mayo Clinic prioritizing private insurance holders over medicare/medicaid holders - and they're a nonprofit.

The whole point being that there is no incentive whatsoever anywhere along the line to lower prices. Imagine instead that hospitals/practices instead set their own prices which were well established and readily available. Now insurance companies choose which hospitals they cover. All insurance would be able to afford less expensive hospitals whereas only more expensive insurance would be able to cover more expensive hospitals. Suddenly there's an incentive for hospitals to charge less instead of charging the maximum possible and then simply accepting a few "secondary" insurance programs in the downtime. To create a fair marketplace here, regulations could require hospitals and practices have open records available to qualified insurers who can determine if they can afford to include the hospital in their coverage.

We spend far more in the US on healthcare than anywhere else in the world, yet our healthcare outcomes on the whole are pretty mediocre relative to the top nations. Our outcomes match our costs only in a handful of specialized areas. So long as money is going to be involved in healthcare (which ideally, I think we should be trying desperately to segue away from) it seems fairly self evident that we should ensure there is an incentive to lower prices.
